description: Why DAC nerds fight about multibit versus delta-sigma, explained at MSN-chat pace. An R-2R ladder you can mismatch, a multibit staircase, a live noise-shaping DFT, an audible bit-depth demo, a reconstruction filter showing the time-frequency tradeoff, and a tube stage you can overdrive into even or odd harmonics. Leans on Schiit Happened and head-fi, cited.
composeNote: This is a recorded conversation. The demos above run live: drag, toggle, and click to hear.
disclosure: Starter draft. The explanations lean on Schiit Happened (Jason Stoddard's book, shared free by the author) and the head-fi threads, paraphrased and cited. The six demos run real math: a quantized staircase, an R-2R ladder you can mismatch, an actual DFT of a noise-shaped signal, a Web Audio tone you can hear at each bit depth, a reconstruction filter showing the time-frequency tradeoff, and a tube stage that turns a sine into even or odd harmonics.

editorial.reader: A curious reader who knows the surface term but wants the mechanism.
editorial.problem: The reader can recognize dac vocabulary without being able to predict what its mechanism will do.
editorial.thesis: The page should leave the reader able to explain dac in plain language and predict its behavior.
evidence: The conversation cites its sources and the demos make the mechanism visible.
The understanding check names common misconceptions and explains every answer.
editorial.uncertainty: The demos teach the model; they do not replace a measurement or a full treatment.

understanding.intro: Before you go pick a side in a DAC forum thread: pop quiz. Five questions, all from the chat above, no stakes.

questions.q: Start with the ladder. A 20-bit R-2R DAC wants resistors matched to about 1 part per million. Why does the bar sit that high?

options.t: the MSB carries half the output, so its error alone has to stay smaller than the smallest step
options.why: Right. Each rung halves the next bit's share, so the big bits carry nearly everything. Let the MSB drift past one step's worth and a code can run backward, the red non-monotonic glitch the tolerance slider produces in the ladder demo.

options.t: each of the 20 bits needs its own distinct resistor value, and that many values are hard to make
options.why: The ladder's whole economy runs the other way: two values only, R and 2R, repeated down the chain. The hard part is matching those repeats, and the MSB rung is where an error costs the most. Scroll back to the ladder demo's lead line.

options.t: the resistors have to switch fast enough to keep up with a sample rate that high
options.why: Speed is delta-sigma's currency, and the page's point is that timing precision comes cheap in digital. A ladder's burden is amplitude precision, exact voltage levels. The tolerance slider bends levels; nothing in that demo touches timing.

options.t: more bits draw more current, and the extra heat drifts the resistor values apart
options.why: Heat and drift are real circuit concerns, but the page pins the cost to matching: the MSB's share against the smallest step. That ratio is why Yggdrasil ships instrumentation parts, the AD5791s that also sit in MRI machines.

questions.q: The noise shaping demo runs the same 3-bit quantizer whether shaping is ON or OFF. What does the feedback loop actually change?

options.t: where the error sits: the same total hash, tilted up and out of the band you can hear
options.why: That's the whole move. The loop high-passes the quantization error, so the floor tilts away from the shaded audible band and piles up in the ultrasonics, where a cheap analog filter wipes it.

options.t: how much error exists: the loop cancels most of the quantization noise outright
options.why: Toggle the demo and look at the right side of the DFT: the floor rises there when shaping is ON. The total error stays roughly the same size and simply relocates above the band. Deletion happens later, at the analog filter.

options.t: the effective bit depth: feedback makes the 3 coarse bits behave like 16 real ones
options.why: Inside the audible band the floor does drop that far, but the mechanism is relocation, and the faint high hiss in the demo's play mode is the receipt. The quantizer stays coarse the whole time; nothing gained bits.

options.t: the tone itself: shaping boosts the signal so it stands clear of the noise floor
options.why: The tone's spike sits at the same height in both modes; only the noise floor moves. The signal path is untouched. The feedback loop filters the error alone, which is what makes the trick so cheap.

questions.q: In the filter demo, dragging sharpness up steepens the frequency wall on the right. What happens on the left, and why is it unavoidable?

options.t: the impulse rings longer, since sharpness in frequency is paid for with length in time
options.why: That's the Fourier tradeoff the whole section rides on. A perfect brick wall at 20 kHz is a sinc that ripples forever in time, and NOS, oversampling, and Moffat's closed-form filter are each a different answer to it.

options.t: nothing changes, a well-designed filter can be sharp in frequency and clean in time
options.why: The two graphs are two views of one object, so tightening the right one lengthens the left one, every time. It's a mathematical constraint, the reason the demo's lead says you cannot tighten both at once.

options.t: the ringing would vanish with better hardware, it comes from cheap filter parts
options.why: The demo is pure math, no hardware anywhere, and it rings anyway. Ringing is the price of the steep wall itself; better parts buy fidelity to a chosen curve and leave the tradeoff standing.

options.t: the click gets quieter, because a longer filter absorbs more of the click's energy
options.why: The click keeps its energy and gets smeared across time instead. Hit play while dragging: each click holds its level but rings longer as the wall sharpens, because the left graph is literally what one click sounds like.

questions.q: The contested ground demo feeds one quiet tone to both architectures. What two different imperfections do the spectra show?

options.t: multibit sprouts spikes at the tone's multiples, delta-sigma keeps one clean spike over a raised floor
options.why: That's the honest core of the debate. Rounding to exact levels bends a quiet wave into harmonic distortion; shaping trades that for a noise floor. Slide to 16-bit and both sink below hearing, which is why the argument never settles.

options.t: multibit shows the raised noise floor, and delta-sigma is the one sprouting harmonic spikes
options.why: Swapped. Rounding to the nearest exact level is what manufactures harmonics, and that's the multibit panel; the shaped floor is delta-sigma's trade. The captions under the two canvases in the demo name each one.

options.t: multibit stays clean down there because its levels are physically exact by construction
options.why: Exact levels are the problem in the soft tail: a quiet wave spans only a few of them, so rounding bends its shape into harmonics. Exactness pays off at full scale and costs you in the quiet passages, which is where the demo lives.

options.t: both show the same imperfection, and the audible gap comes entirely from the filters
options.why: The filter carries real audible character, the chat grants that, but this demo isolates a mechanical difference underneath: harmonics on one side, noise on the other. Same tone, two flavors of imperfection, pick yours.

questions.q: Last one, on warmth. Why does the tube curve read as full while the hard clip reads as buzz, when both are just distortion?

options.t: the tube's lopsided curve grows mostly the 2nd harmonic, the symmetric clip cancels evens and stacks the odds
options.why: That's the tell. The 2nd harmonic IS the octave, the most consonant interval there is, so the ear reads fuller. Symmetry cancels the evens, and the odd stack (3rd, 5th, 7th) climbs toward the square-wave buzz of a signal slammed into its rails.

options.t: tubes roll off the harsh treble frequencies, while transistor-style clipping leaves all of them in
options.why: The tube mode adds content, a new harmonic above the note, and the tone's own treble never moves. Watch the spectrum bars: 2x grows as you push the drive. Warmth here is additive, a stacked octave, per the demo's lead.

options.t: tubes add no distortion at all, and that untouched clean transfer is what people call smooth
options.why: The meter says otherwise: the tube curve raises THD, and some listeners chase exactly that reading as warmth. The page's point is that WHICH harmonics grow decides the character, so more distortion can still sound fuller.

options.t: odd harmonics are the consonant ones, since the 3rd harmonic sits closest to the original note
options.why: Consonance tracks intervals, and the 2nd harmonic lands exactly one octave up, the friendliest interval available. The odd stack is what builds a square wave. Flip the demo to hard clip and listen to where that dial ends.

messages.html: every dac debate online collapses into multibit versus delta-sigma, and everyone gets religious about it. what's the actual engineering difference, underneath the tribalism?

Both turn a stream of numbers into a voltage. They split on how to rebuild the wave from the samples. Multibit builds each sample as one exact level. Delta-sigma approximates that level with a coarse switch running very fast, then hides the leftover error where your ears can't reach. Two roads to the same clean output.
start with multibit. that's the one that works the way I'd naively guess.

It does. An N-bit value selects one of 2N voltages, and a resistor ladder (R-2R) sums the bits into exactly that level. A 16-bit sample picks one of 65,536 voltages. The raw output is a staircase, one flat step per sample, which a filter then smooths into a curve.

demo.bar: the staircase · drag the bit depth
demo.html:
A multibit DAC builds each sample as one exact voltage, chosen from 2N levels a resistor ladder defines. Drag the bit depth: more bits means a finer staircase, closer to the smooth wave underneath.

Hit play and drag the bit depth: at 3-bit the quantization hash is loud, and it melts off as the staircase gets finer. Same tone, same sine, just more levels.

messages.html: back up. how does a ladder of resistors actually turn the bits into that exact voltage?

It is a chain of voltage dividers built from only two resistor values, R and 2R, one rung per bit. The trick: from any rung, the resistance looking back toward the smaller bits always works out to R, so each rung halves the contribution of the one above it. The most significant bit lands Vref/2 at the output, the next Vref/4, then Vref/8, on down. Switch a bit to Vref and it adds its rung's share, so the total is Vref times the binary value over 2N, all from two resistor values repeated.

demo.bar: the R-2R ladder · toggle bits, then add resistor error
demo.html:
An R-2R ladder turns N bits into one voltage from just two resistor values. Each raised bit adds half the previous bit's share: the MSB adds Vref/2, the next Vref/4, and so on. Toggle the bits, then crank the resistor tolerance and watch the transfer curve bend.

Vout = 0.500 Vref

The transfer curve over all 64 codes, ideal (straight) against actual. Errors in the big bits bend the line; push the tolerance and a step can run backward (red), a non-monotonic glitch. That is why a 20-bit ladder wants parts matched to about 1 part per million: the MSB resistor alone has to beat the size of the smallest step. Play a tone through the ladder and raise the tolerance: the bending curve turns into audible harmonic distortion, worst where a step runs backward.

messages.html: so a tiny error in the big bits wrecks it. that's where the cost goes.

Exactly. Those resistors have to be matched to brutal tolerances, which is instrumentation hardware, not audio-grade parts. Schiit's Yggdrasil runs a quad of 20-bit Analog Devices AD5791 ladders, the same parts that sit in MRI machines, because ordinary chips can't hold that line.
ok, delta-sigma. how do you get clean audio out of a switch that's basically on or off?

Speed plus a feedback loop. Run a 1-bit quantizer at 64 to 256 times the audio rate, and feed the quantization error back so the output works out to X(z)·z-1 + E(z)·(1 - z-1). That (1 - z-1) is a high-pass filter on the error: it shoves the noise up into ultrasonic frequencies, out of the band you hear, where a cheap analog filter wipes it. You trade amplitude precision for timing precision, which is exactly what digital is good at.

demo.html:
A delta-sigma DAC runs a coarse quantizer fast, with a feedback loop that shapes the quantization noise. Toggle it: the same 3-bit quantizer either way, but shaping pushes the error up out of the band you can hear (shaded).

3-bit quantizer, 1st-order shaping

Spectrum of the quantizer output. The spike is the tone; the floor is quantization noise. Shaping tilts that floor up and away from the shaded audible band. Play it and toggle shaping: OFF is a grainy in-band hash, ON pushes that hash up into a faint high hiss and clears the tone.

messages.html: huh. same coarse quantizer either way, but shaping pulls the floor down inside the band. that's the whole move?

That's the whole move. Stack more integrators and the term becomes (1 - z-1)2 or 3 for a steeper tilt. Because the quantizer is just a fast switch, it stays cheap and very linear, which is why nearly every DAC chip on the market (ESS, AKM, Cirrus) is delta-sigma and posts excellent THD and SNR.
both end up as a stairstep or a 1-bit stream. how does that become a smooth analog wave? something filters it, right?

The reconstruction filter, and it carries the other big optimization. The ideal one is a sinc, a perfect brick wall at 20 kHz, but a brick wall in frequency is an endless ripple in time. That is the Fourier tradeoff: you get sharpness in frequency or cleanliness in time, and tightening one loosens the other. A fast, sharp filter kills the images just above the band but rings; a slow filter rings less but rolls off some treble and lets a little imaging through. NOS DACs skip the filter (no ringing, images and all); oversampling first pushes the images far up, so a gentle filter can finish without ringing much.

demo.html:
A windowed-sinc reconstruction filter. Drag the sharpness: more taps steepen the frequency wall on the right, and the impulse response on the left rings longer to pay for it. You cannot tighten both at once.

Left: the impulse response in time, the sinc and its ringing. Right: the frequency response, flat through the shaded audio band and rolling off near Nyquist. A sharper wall on the right means longer ringing on the left. Play the click train and drag sharpness: the left graph IS what one click sounds like, so a sharper filter makes each click ring longer.

messages.html: so the filter shape is a taste call as much as a number on a spec sheet.

Largely yes, and a lot of the audible gap between two competent DACs lives right here, more than in the last decimal of THD. It is also Mike Moffat's whole angle: instead of the stock windowed-sinc he ships a custom closed-form filter, the kind of choice a measurement cannot fully settle.
so if delta-sigma measures better and costs less, why does multibit still have a cult around it?

Two honest reasons. First, coarse bits are audible when nothing shapes them away, and some listeners argue the modulator's behavior on quiet passages and decay sounds different in ways a steady-tone measurement won't show. Second, Mike Moffat, the digital half of Schiit, bet a company on multibit, the ladders plus that closed-form filter, and built a following that hears a difference. The measurable gap is tiny and often below audibility; the preference is real to the people who hold it and hard to reduce to one number.
I get the theory, but I still can't reconcile what people MEAN by the multibit sound versus delta-sigma. can you make that difference concrete?

The honest place it lives is low-level linearity: the soft tail of a note, where only the bottom bits are working. Multibit rounds to its nearest exact level, which down there bends the wave into harmonic distortion. Delta-sigma keeps the level honest on average and trades that for a shaped noise floor. Same quiet tone, two different imperfections. Here they are side by side, as spectra you can also play.

demo.html:
Where the multibit-versus-delta-sigma argument actually lives: a quiet tone, the soft tail of a note, where only the lowest bits are working. Drag the bit depth. Multibit rounds to its nearest exact level, which at low level bends the wave into harmonic distortion; delta-sigma keeps the level honest on average but rides a shaped noise floor. Same tone, two flavors of imperfection.

multibit (round to level)
delta-sigma (noise-shaped)

Both spectra are the same quiet tone. Multibit sprouts harmonic spikes at the tone's multiples (distortion); delta-sigma stays a single clean spike on a raised noise floor (no harmonics). Push the bit depth toward 16 and both shrink below hearing.

messages.html: so multibit adds harmonics, delta-sigma adds noise, and by 16-bit both basically vanish.

That is the whole reconciliation: pick your imperfection. Harmonic distortion can read as warmth or as grit; a noise floor reads as clean, though some hear it as veiling. On good 24-bit gear both sit below audibility, so the preference comes down to taste and system matching rather than a measurement. Real multibit DACs usually dither as well, which trades their distortion for a noise floor of their own and narrows the gap further.

demo.html:
Quantization noise is audible when the bit depth is low. Click to hear a 440 Hz tone quantized to each depth (about a second each, through your speakers).

Same tone, fewer levels. At 2-bit the error is loud hash; by 16-bit it's gone. Delta-sigma keeps the bits low and moves that hash above 20 kHz instead.

messages.html: yeah, I can hear the hash at 2-bit, and it's gone by 16. and delta-sigma just shoves that hash above 20k instead of spending money to delete it.

Right. Multibit pays in hardware to make every level physically exact. Delta-sigma pays in cleverness to make the errors inaudible. Both arrive at clean sound; they just disagree about where to put the hard part, and the filter is where a lot of the audible character is decided.
one more, since you keep landing on that word. "warmth" is the exact thing people say about tube amps. is the multibit version literally the same effect a tube has?

Same family, and it is worth seeing why. Both bend the wave into harmonics; the character is set by which ones. A gentle, lopsided curve, the kind a single tube makes, adds mostly the 2nd harmonic, which sits exactly one octave above the note, so your ear reads it as fuller rather than dirty. Drive the same tone into a hard, symmetric clip and the even harmonics cancel, leaving the odd ones (3rd, 5th, 7th) that climb toward a square wave, the buzz of a signal slammed flat into its rails. Push the curve below and watch which harmonics grow.

demo.bar: tube warmth · drive a sine into the curve
demo.html:
Past the DAC, the signal meets an amplifier, and this is where "warmth" gets built on purpose. A single tube's transfer curve is gently lopsided, so it grows mostly the 2nd harmonic, one octave up. A hard, symmetric clip cancels the even harmonics and grows odd ones instead, heading for a square wave. Drive it, switch the curve, and watch the spectrum; hit play to hear it.

Left: the transfer curve, output against input, the straight dashed line being no distortion at all. The tube curve bows more on one side (asymmetric, even harmonics); the clip flattens both rails alike (symmetric, odd harmonics). Middle: what that does to a sine. Bottom: the harmonics, each labeled by its multiple of the note. 2× is the octave that reads as warmth; the odd stack (3×, 5×, 7×...) is the square-wave buzz. Real tubes add some higher-order even harmonics too; this isolates the dominant 2nd. Hit play, then keep driving and toggling: the tone shifts in real time, no need to re-press.

messages.html: so the 2nd harmonic IS the octave, that's why it reads as musical, and hard clipping just collapses into a square, all odd harmonics. the asymmetry is the whole tell.

That is the tell, and it is the same axis the DAC argument rides. A little 2nd harmonic is what some people are chasing when a multibit ladder or a tube stage "sounds warm," even as the meter reports higher THD. A square wave is just the far end of that dial: every bit of headroom spent, nothing left but the odd harmonics.

clearest version of this I've read. thanks.
